ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 2 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Julius Caesar

code.originalText: Two-week follow-up with the neurology consultation: EEG, MRI, vascular imaging, echocardiogram, and monitor reviewed; diagnosis made and treatment started

text.paragraph: Two-week follow-up after recurrent spells of collapse; test results and neurology consultation today. [S]

Julius Caesar returns two weeks after his first visit. He saw Dr. Lindqvist-Adeyemi of neurology this morning. He has had no further spell, though he woke once from a vivid, frightening dream, confused for a minute or two, which happens every few weeks. The EEG showed intermittent left temporal sharp waves. The MRI showed no new stroke but an old small infarct in the left posterior temporal lobe and moderate small-vessel white matter changes, with no tumor, vascular malformation, or cyst. CT angiography showed a small calcified plaque at the left carotid bifurcation, under 30 percent. The echocardiogram showed mild left ventricular thickening, no clot, and no shunt. The 14-day monitor showed sinus rhythm throughout; the one event he marked, light-headedness on standing up quickly, was in sinus rhythm. He has taken lisinopril every morning without cough or dizziness but did not keep the home blood pressure log. He has not driven, has showered rather than bathed, and has not ridden. He wants to know what the spells are and when he can drive again. [S]

list.item:
Recurrent transient episodes of collapse: resolved into a diagnosis (R56.9). The spells are seizures. A rising feeling, staring with lip-smacking, a bitten tongue, and confusion lasting many minutes afterwards point to seizures rather than syncope, and the ECG, the orthostatic blood pressures, the echocardiogram, and two weeks of monitoring show no cardiac cause. A transient ischemic attack causes a sudden loss of function lasting minutes, not loss of awareness with jerking and a long confused recovery, and the arteries show no significant narrowing. The EEG and the MRI agree on a left temporal source. [S]
Resolved: the diagnosis is recorded as focal epilepsy (PRB-004) from the chronic infarct (PRB-005).

Focal epilepsy with a structural vascular cause (G40.209). Under the ILAE 2017 classification: focal impaired-awareness seizures with automatisms, one evolving to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, with a structural (vascular) cause. Three unprovoked seizures meet the ILAE definition of epilepsy, and the infarct and the EEG both predict recurrence. Treatment is advised, as Dr. Lindqvist-Adeyemi recommends. [S]
Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily from today.
Teaching about irritability, low mood, and drowsiness, which usually settle; call at once with any thoughts of self-harm.
Seizure diary; no missed doses.
PHQ-9 at the four-week visit.

Chronic left temporal cortical infarct (I69.398). An ischemic infarct that was never recognized as a stroke but now causes seizures. Treated with secondary stroke prevention. The echocardiogram and the first monitor found no source of embolism. [S]
Aspirin 81 mg daily.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at bedtime; lipid panel at 4 to 12 weeks.
A second ambulatory monitor from today for four more weeks, to look for atrial fibrillation.
STOP-Bang score 3 (blood pressure, age, male sex): home sleep apnea test ordered.
MoCA at the next visit.

Hypertension (I10). 140/88 mmHg on lisinopril 10 mg, down from 152/94; still above the target of 130/80. Potassium 4.5 mmol/L and creatinine 1.02 mg/dL, up 4 percent: safe to continue. [S]
Continue lisinopril 10 mg.
Home blood pressure log twice daily with a memory cuff; a second medicine at the next visit if still above target.

Hyperlipidemia (E78.5). LDL 158 mg/dL; the target after an ischemic infarct with carotid plaque is below 70 mg/dL. [S]
Atorvastatin 80 mg as above; report muscle aches.
